The measured noise power spectral density of the drain current shows that the LFN in a-ZnON TFTs obeys the classical 1/<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$f$ </tex-math></inline-formula> noise theory, i.e., it is proportional to 1/<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$f^{\mathrm {\gamma }}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> with <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\gamma \sim 1$ </tex-math></inline-formula> in the frequency range from 10 Hz to 1 kHz. The LFN from the a-ZnON TFT is successfully interpreted by the correlated number fluctuation-mobility fluctuation model. The near-interface dielectric trap density (<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{T})$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and the Coulomb scattering coefficient (<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\alpha _{S})$ </tex-math></inline-formula> extracted from the measured LFN in a-ZnON TFTs are similar to those from the previously reported values for amorphous indium–gallium–zinc oxide TFTs. The relatively large values of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{T}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\alpha _{S}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> from the a-ZnON TFTs formed under O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>-rich environment are mainly attributed to the high degree of disorder of the a-ZnON channel layer caused by the energetically broad and high density of subgap tail states.

articleTitle: Investigation of Gate Direct-Current and Fluctuations in Organic p-Type Thin-Film Transistors
abstract: Investigation of gate dielectric conduction properties in organic p-type staggered thin-film transistors is reported by means of direct-current, capacitance-voltage, and noise measurements. Results suggest that transport in the CYTOPTM gate dielectric is dominated, at low currents, by Schottky conduction due to the emission at the aluminum gate interface through a barrier φ<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">B</sub> ≈ 1 eV, while is limited, at higher currents, by space-charge conduction in the trap-limited regime with an effective mobility μ<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">θ</sub> estimated in the order of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-9</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/(Vs). Gate current noise follows a 1/f law and it is found to be proportional to I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup><sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">G</sub>, which is inconsistent with the commonly assumed mobility fluctuation. Traps responsible for gate noise are dielectric-bulk traps, not located at the semiconductor interface, since the gate noise is found to be uncorrelated with drain noise.

articleTitle: Organic Single-Crystal Transistors and Circuits on Ultra-Fine Au Wires With Diameters as Small as 15  $\mu \text{m}$  via Jigsaw Puzzle Method
abstract: A novel jigsaw puzzle method was developed to fabricate the high-performance CuPc and F<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">16</sub>CuPc organic single-crystal field-effect transistors and circuits on ultra-fine and flexible Au wires with diameters as small as 15 μm. This method weakens the effect of fiber size on the device-fabrication process and provides a simple way to realize organic single-crystal complementary circuits on ultra-fine fibers. The resulting high-performance miniaturized fiber-shaped devices with extremely small diameters have strong potential for the applications in wearable and implantable electronics.

articleTitle: Origin of Initial Rapid Cell Current Reduction in Non-Volatile One-Time Programming Memory
abstract: The fast bit cell current (BCC) reduction in a one-time programming (OTP) device during high-temperature annealing will severely decrease the data retention (DR) capability. It is found that negative bias temperature instability-like degradation is responsible for this fast BCC shift, which is different from the well-known DR mechanism. The rapid floating gate charge diminution at the initial stage can be attributed to the recombination by hydrogen species as a result of the depassivation of Si-H bonds at the Si/SiO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> interface. Our experiments show that the BCC reduction rate follows a power-law time dependence t<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-0.73</sup>, which is in agreement with a simple analytical model based on interface state (N<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">it</sub>) generation and floating-gate voltage shift. These observations pave the way for further OTP DR reliability improvement.

articleTitle: Organic Relay Carry Generator and Logic Gates
abstract: This letter demonstrates that a single organic micrometer-scale relay can easily generate a carry for four input bits and perform basic Boolean operations for two input bits.

articleTitle: Accurate Estimation Technique of Low-Frequency Noise in NAND Flash Cell Array
abstract: We propose a technique to accurately estimate low-frequency noise (LFN) of a NAND flash cell. When we measure the LFN of a particular cell in NAND cell array, parasitic resistance and noise due to other cells have high potential to degrade the accuracy of this measurement. We derive small signal equivalent circuit of a NAND flash cell array and then, de-embed the effects of the above parasitic components. We perform this estimation in sub-20-nm NAND flash technology. The results clearly show the necessity of our proposed estimation technique.

articleTitle: Low-Field Transport in Bovine Serum Albumin Conjugated ZnO Nanoparticle Networks
abstract: A Au/bovine serum albumin (BSA)–ZnO (n-type nanoparticles)/Au system is investigated for its transport properties using electrical (<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$I$ </tex-math></inline-formula>–<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$V$ </tex-math></inline-formula>) characterization in conjunction with spectroscopy techniques for cost-effective power-efficient biosensing. Temperature-dependent variation in different conduction mechanisms is observed with Au/ZnO/Au system as reference. Schottky emission dominates the carrier transport with defect-assisted tunneling and Poole–Frenkel hopping contributing peripherally. The distribution of defect states within the ZnO bandgap appears to be responsible for such low-field conduction characteristics along with the surface dipole effect of the BSA, which modulates barrier height and, consequently, carrier population in the ZnO nanoparticles.

articleTitle: IEEE Robert Bosch Micro and Nano Electro Mechanical Systems Award
abstract: Explains the specific criteria for the Robert Bosch Micro and Nano Electro Mechanical Systems Award. The Robert Bosch Micro and Nano Electro Mechanical Systems Award was established by the IEEE Electron Devices Society in 2014 to recognize and honor advances in the invention, design, and/or fabrication of micro- or nanoelectromechanical systems and/or devices. The contributions to be honored by this award should be innovative and useful for practical applications. This award is sponsored by the IEEE Electron Devices Society with financial support from Robert Bosch LLC. It is intended that the award will be presented annually to an individual or to as many as three individuals whose achievements and contributions are judged to meet the selection criteria for the award. The award will be presented at an IEEE conference of the winner‚s choice. It is not necessary for the recipient(s) to be a member(s) of IEEE. The recipient will receive a US$10,000 honorarium (which includes up to $3,000 of travel expenses for international travel and $1,500 of travel expenses for domestic travel), a bronze medal, and a certificate. In the event that more than one awardee is selected, the cash honorarium will be equally divided among the recipients. Each recipient will receive a bronze medal and a certificate. Please consider nominating your colleagues for this award by visiting the EDS website (http://eds.ieee.org/robertbosch- micro-and-nano-electro-mechanical-systems-award.html).
